questions.enonce_markdown:
The polynomial $P(x)$ is such that $P(x) \equiv ax^3 - 3x^2 + bx + 6$. Given that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $P(x)$ and that when $P(x)$ is divided by $(x-1)$ the remainder is $-6$.

(a) Find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$.

(b) Hence, solve the equation $P(x) = 0$. (7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a)** By the factor theorem, $(x+2)$ is a factor of $P(x)$, so $P(-2) = 0$. By the remainder theorem, the remainder on division by $(x-1)$ is $P(1) = -6$.

$$P(-2) = -8a - 12 - 2b + 6 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -8a - 2b = 6 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4a + b = -3.$$

$$P(1) = a - 3 + b + 6 = -6 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a + b = -9.$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first: $3a = 6$, so $a = 2$. Then $b = -9 - 2 = -11$.

$$\boxed{a = 2,\quad b = -11}$$

Check: $P(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 11x + 6$, so $P(-2) = -16 - 12 + 22 + 6 = 0$ and $P(1) = 2 - 3 - 11 + 6 = -6$.

**(b)** Since $(x+2)$ is a factor, divide $2x^3 - 3x^2 - 11x + 6$ by $(x+2)$:

$$2x^3 - 3x^2 - 11x + 6 = (x+2)(2x^2 - 7x + 3).$$

Expanding to check: $(x+2)(2x^2 - 7x + 3) = 2x^3 - 7x^2 + 3x + 4x^2 - 14x + 6 = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 11x + 6$. Correct.

Factorise the quadratic: $2x^2 - 7x + 3 = (2x - 1)(x - 3)$. Hence

$$P(x) = (x+2)(2x-1)(x-3) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x = -2,\ \ x = \tfrac12,\ \ x = 3.$$

$$\boxed{x = -2,\quad x = \tfrac12,\quad x = 3}$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two statements $p$ and $q$ are given by

$p$: Comfort studies hard.

$q$: She will pass the examination.

Write out the following propositions in simple English.

(c) $p \Rightarrow q$

(d) $\sim p \Rightarrow \sim q$

(e) $\sim (p \Rightarrow q)$ (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The symbol $\sim$ means "not" and $\Rightarrow$ means "implies" (if ... then ...).

**(c)** $p \Rightarrow q$: *If Comfort studies hard, then she will pass the examination.*

**(d)** $\sim p \Rightarrow \sim q$: *If Comfort does not study hard, then she will not pass the examination.* This is the **inverse** of $p \Rightarrow q$; it is not logically equivalent to it.

**(e)** $\sim(p \Rightarrow q)$: *It is not true that if Comfort studies hard she will pass the examination.* The implication $p \Rightarrow q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false, so $\sim(p \Rightarrow q)$ is equivalent to $p \wedge \sim q$. In simple English: *Comfort studies hard but she does not pass the examination.*
